column1:
plastic items made to be used once, e.g. straws, cups, bags

plural; neutral; always hyphenate single-use · Grammar: inversion conditional

column1:
designing products so that they break or go out of date quickly

Not only does _____ waste resources, but it also forces consumers to replace devices that could easily be repaired.
column2:
planned obsolescence
Not only does planned obsolescence waste resources, but it also forces consumers to replace devices that could easily be repaired.

a system in which products and materials are reused, repaired, and recycled rather than thrown away

the circular economy

a landfill

column1:
the materials used to wrap goods

packaging

column1:
trash produced by homes

household waste

U: NOT household wastes · Grammar: the more…, the more…

column1:
a policy that makes manufacturers pay for collecting and recycling what they sell

Under _____, the cost of collecting packaging should be borne by manufacturers rather than taxpayers.
column2:
extended producer responsibility
Under extended producer responsibility, the cost of collecting packaging should be borne by manufacturers rather than taxpayers.
U; formal; abbreviation EPR · Grammar: modal passive

thrown-away electronic devices

rotted food and yard waste used to feed soil

compost

produce trash

generate waste

prevent trash from being created in the first place

reduce waste at the source

get rid of sth, especially safely

formal; NOT dispose sth (needs of); noun: disposal (U) · Grammar: modal passive

the percentage of waste that is recycled

Officials should have realized that _____ would stall once China stopped accepting foreign plastic waste in 2018.

recycling rates

C, plural; rates rise / fall / stall · Grammar: modal perfect

cups designed to be thrown away after one use

disposable cups

a bottle you can use again and again

put different kinds of waste in different bins

more wrapping than is needed

excessive packaging

U; neutral · Grammar: sentential relative

column1:
a legal right to have products fixed, with access to parts and manuals

_____ is expected to reduce e-waste by making spare parts and manuals available to everyone.

the right to repair

make a product last longer

a charge for each ton of trash buried

column1:
leaving trash illegally in a public place

illegal dumping

the way people usually shop and use products

consumer habits

put sth in the trash

get rid of, abolish

consume less of sth

finish all of sth

use sth up

neutral · Grammar: modal passive

column1:
become useless through use

wear out

column1:
remove dirt or trash from a place

clean sth up

neutral; noun: a cleanup (C; BrE: a clean-up) · Grammar: no matter / however

column1:
throughout a product's whole life, from making to disposal

the order of priorities for handling waste

reduce, reuse, recycle

people forget what they cannot see

out of sight, out of mind

the idea that whoever causes pollution should pay for it

Only by enforcing _____ can governments make manufacturers cover the true cost of disposal.

the polluter pays principle

column1:
made to be durable

built to last

an amount too small to make a difference

be wasted, not used

go to waste

manage with what you already have instead of buying more

make do (with sth)

materials that break down naturally / that can turn into compost

biodegradable / compostable materials

waste that does not decay naturally

non-biodegradable waste

tiny pieces of plastic, smaller than 5 millimeters

microplastics

plural; neutral · Grammar: negative inversion

plastic waste that harms nature, especially trash in the ocean

plastic pollution / marine debris

waste that can harm people or the environment, e.g. chemicals and batteries

contaminate sth / contamination

collection of trash or recycling from outside people's homes

curbside pickup

a recycling plant

burning waste; a facility that burns waste

incineration / an incinerator

a facility that burns trash to produce electricity or heat

column1:

column1:
edible food that is thrown away

food waste

U: NOT food wastes; food scraps (plural) = peels and leftovers · Grammar: unreal past

column1:
cheap, trendy clothing that is produced quickly and thrown away soon

fast fashion

U; neutral; fast-fashion brands (hyphenated before a noun) · Grammar: the more…, the more…

column1:
buying and using more than is necessary or sustainable

overconsumption

U; formal; verb: overconsume · Grammar: mixed conditional

a way of living that aims to send nothing to a landfill

column1:
turning old items into new products of higher value

upcycling

U; verb: upcycle sth · Grammar: sentential relative

column1:
a store where customers fill their own containers with products sold by weight

a refill store

C; also a zero-waste store; BrE: a refill shop · Grammar: inversion conditional

column1:
products designed to last a long time, e.g. cars and appliances

Despite costing more upfront, _____ such as well-made appliances often save consumers money in the long run.

durable goods

plural; formal; adj durable = long-lasting · Grammar: concession

column1:
trash left on the ground in public places; collect it

Every spring, volunteers _____ along the highway, thereby saving the state considerable cleanup costs.

litter / pick up litter

buy sth that someone else has already owned and used

buy sth secondhand

give sth you no longer need to a younger person

hand sth down

neutral; noun: a hand-me-down (C) · Grammar: the more…, the more…

long-term changes in the Earth's climate, especially warming caused by human activity

_____ is widely thought to be the main reason why harvests in southern Europe are becoming less reliable.

climate change

U, no article: NOT the climate change · Grammar: impersonal passive

column1:
the rise in the Earth's average temperature

column2:
global warming
The faster global warming progresses, the more quickly mountain glaciers shrink and disappear.
U, no article · Grammar: the more…, the more…

column1:
carbon dioxide released into the air, e.g. from burning fuel

column2:
carbon emissions

plural; also greenhouse gas emissions · Grammar: cleft sentence

the total amount of carbon dioxide a person or organization causes

a carbon footprint

C; reduce / shrink / calculate your carbon footprint · Grammar: unreal past

a tax on fuels or products according to how much carbon they release

Were governments to introduce _____, polluting industries would have a strong incentive to cut their emissions.

a carbon tax

C; introduce / impose a carbon tax · Grammar: inversion conditional

column1:
coal, oil, and gas

Not only do _____ heat the planet, but they also pollute the air that millions of people breathe.
column2:
fossil fuels

C, usually plural · Grammar: negative inversion

column1:
unusually severe heat waves, storms, floods, and droughts

column2:
extreme weather

U; C in extreme weather events · Grammar: so/such… that

a state in which a country removes as much carbon as it emits

net zero

U, no article; reach / achieve net zero · Grammar: modal passive

making a company or product seem more environmentally friendly than it really is

greenwashing

U; neutral; verb: to greenwash · Grammar: participle clause

paying for projects such as tree planting to "cancel out" your emissions

carbon offsetting

U; noun an offset (C) · Grammar: concession

a period of unusually hot weather

a heat wave

deal with the problem seriously

neutral; also combat / address (formal) · Grammar: relative: whose / whereby / in which

reduce the amount of greenhouse gases released

cut emissions

neutral; also curb emissions (formal) · Grammar: result clause with thereby/thus

set a target

legally binding targets

make polluters pay for each ton of CO2 they emit

neutral; noun: carbon pricing (U) · Grammar: cleft sentence

a collective effort
